title: On vs l'on
goal: By the end of this lesson you can use on in all its meanings with correct agreement, recognise and use the formal written l'on, and switch between written nous and spoken on.

body: *On* is always grammatically third-person singular: *on parle, on va, on est*. But it has three meanings.

1. People in general: *Au Québec, on mange de la tourtière à Noël.* 2. Someone, an unknown person (often the English passive): *On m'a volé mon vélo.* = My bike was stolen. 3. We, in everyday speech: *On part à huit heures.*
learn.tip: When English uses 'it is said', 'they say' or a passive with no agent, French reaches for on.

body: The verb stays singular, but adjectives and past participles with *être* usually agree with the real people: *On est contents. On est allées au cinéma* (if all women). This agreement is accepted by all modern grammars.
The matching reflexive is *se*: *on se lève*. The matching possessive in speech is *notre/nos*: *On a vendu notre maison.* The stressed pronoun is *nous*: *Nous, on reste.*

*L'on* is the same word as *on* with an old article (*on* comes from Latin *homo*, 'man'). Today it is a stylistic choice in careful writing, mainly to avoid a vowel clash (hiatus) or an awkward sound.
It appears after *et, ou, où, si, que, lorsque, quoi*: *si l'on veut*, *où l'on vit*, *ce que l'on dit*. After *que*, it also avoids the sound *qu'on*, which some writers find inelegant.
Never use *l'on* before a word starting with *l*: write *si on le sait*, not *si l'on le sait*. *L'on* at the very start of a sentence is very rare today. In speech, it sounds bookish or official.
learn.tip: L'on is never required. When in doubt, plain on is always correct.

body: In formal texts, *on* is fine in the sense 'people in general' or 'someone': *On estime que 80 % des Québécois parlent français à la maison.* Avoid *on* = 'we' in an essay or letter; write *nous* instead.
When *on* is indefinite, the possessive is *son/sa/ses* and the reflexive *soi*: *On doit respecter ses engagements. On est mieux chez soi.*

examples.fr: Au Québec, on mange de la tourtière à Noël.
examples.en: In Quebec, people eat meat pie at Christmas.

examples.fr: On m'a volé mon vélo hier soir.
examples.en: My bike was stolen last night.

examples.fr: On a annulé la réunion de lundi.
On part à huit heures, ça te va?
examples.en: We're leaving at eight, does that work for you?

examples.fr: On est contents de vous voir.
Ma sœur et moi, on est allées au marché Jean-Talon.
examples.en: My sister and I went to the Jean-Talon market.

examples.fr: On a repeint notre cuisine en bleu.
On doit toujours respecter ses engagements.
examples.en: One must always keep one's commitments.

examples.fr: On n'est jamais si bien que chez soi.
examples.note: indefinite on → soi; note n' after on before a vowel

examples.fr: Si l'on considère les chiffres, la situation s'améliore.
examples.en: If one considers the figures, the situation is improving.

examples.fr: C'est un pays où l'on parle deux langues officielles.
examples.en: It's a country where two official languages are spoken.

examples.fr: Ce que l'on croit savoir n'est pas toujours vrai.
examples.en: What we think we know isn't always true.

examples.fr: Si on le lui demande, il acceptera.
examples.en: If we ask him, he'll accept.

examples.fr: On estime que la population dépassera neuf millions.
examples.en: It is estimated that the population will exceed nine million.

examples.fr: Lorsque l'on arrive à Québec par le fleuve, on voit d'abord le Château Frontenac.
examples.en: When you arrive in Quebec City by the river, you first see the Château Frontenac.
examples.note: l'on after lorsque, then plain on

quebec.intro: In Quebec speech, on has almost completely replaced nous as a subject; nous survives as a stressed form, usually as 'nous autres'. L'on is a purely written, formal marker: you'll see it in Le Devoir, government documents and speeches, never in conversation.

items.note: nous as a subject sounds stiff in conversation
nous autres = stressed 'we'; icitte = ici, very informal

items.qc: Vous autres, vous venez-tu avec nous autres?
items.en: Are you guys coming with us?
items.note: vous autres = plural 'you'; -tu marks a yes/no question; informal
l'on would sound bookish in speech
eux autres; y = ils; ne dropped; informal

drills.q: 'On m'a volé mon portefeuille' is best translated as…
drills.why: Indefinite on often corresponds to an English passive.

drills.q: Ma femme et moi, on est ___ hier. (arriver)
drills.why: On = we (a man and a woman) → masculine plural agreement is usual.
Avoid l'on before a word starting with l: si on le sait.

drills.q: In a formal essay, 'we' should usually be…
drills.why: On = we is informal; formal writing uses nous.

drills.q: C'est la ville où ___ on a grandi. (formal 'l')
drills.en: It's the city where we grew up.
drills.why: L'on after où in formal writing.

drills.q: On est ___ de vous revoir. (content, two women speaking)
drills.en: We're happy to see you again.
drills.why: Agreement with the real subject: feminine plural.
The reflexive pronoun for on is se.

drills.q: On n'est jamais mieux que chez ___.
drills.en: You're never better off than at home.

drills.why: French prefers on over a passive.

vocab.ex: Si l'on compare les deux textes…
Il faut avoir confiance en soi.
On estime que le projet coûtera cher.
On mange de la tourtière à Noël.
C'est la ville où l'on a grandi.

pron.tip: Liaison: [o-NA]. The nasal stays nasal and the n is added.
Sounds the same as on est pas: [o-NÈ-pa]; the n' is heard only through the liaison.
[si-LON-veu]; the l softens the clash between si and on.
[o-nè kon-TAN]; no change in sound for the plural.

dialogue.fr: As-tu écouté le discours du maire hier?
dialogue.en: Did you listen to the mayor's speech yesterday?

dialogue.fr: Oui. Il a dit : « Si l'on veut une ville plus verte, il faut agir maintenant. »
dialogue.en: Yes. He said: 'If we want a greener city, we must act now.'

dialogue.fr: « Si l'on veut »? Personne ne parle comme ça!
dialogue.en: 'If one wants'? Nobody talks like that!

dialogue.fr: C'est un discours officiel, c'est normal. Nous autres, on dirait juste « si on veut ».
dialogue.en: It's an official speech, that's normal. We'd just say 'if we want'.

dialogue.fr: On va planter dix mille arbres, et on a annulé le projet de stationnement.
dialogue.en: Ten thousand trees will be planted, and the parking project has been cancelled.

dialogue.fr: Bonne nouvelle! On est contents, nous autres, dans le quartier.
dialogue.en: Good news! We're happy about that in the neighbourhood.

questions.q: Why did the mayor say 'si l'on veut'?
How many trees will be planted?

speak.prompt: Describe three customs where you live using on = people in general.
speak.model: Au Québec, on enlève ses bottes en entrant chez quelqu'un. On mange de la tire sur la neige au printemps. Et le 1er juillet, on déménage!

speak.prompt: Tell what you and your family did last weekend using on, with correct agreement.
speak.model: Samedi, on est allés à la cabane à sucre. On était un peu fatigués, mais on s'est bien amusés. Dimanche, on est restés à la maison.

speak.prompt: Read this formal sentence aloud, then say it casually: 'Si l'on observe ce que l'on mange, on comprend beaucoup de choses.'
speak.model: Formel : Si l'on observe ce que l'on mange, on comprend beaucoup de choses. / Familier : Si on regarde ce qu'on mange, on comprend ben des affaires.

write.prompt: Write a short formal paragraph (5–6 sentences) for a city newsletter about recycling. Use on (general) and l'on at least twice, and nous once.
write.model: Chaque année, on jette des tonnes de déchets qui pourraient être recyclés. Si l'on veut réduire ce gaspillage, chacun doit faire sa part. On rappelle que le bac bleu accepte le papier, le carton, le verre et le plastique. Ce que l'on oublie souvent, c'est que les sacs de plastique doivent être regroupés dans un seul sac. Nous comptons sur votre collaboration. Ensemble, on peut faire la différence.

quiz.why: On takes a singular verb: on va, on est.
L'on is a stylistic marker of careful written French.
Singular verb, plural participle when on = we.

quiz.q: Why might a writer prefer 'que l'on' to 'qu'on'?
quiz.why: It's a matter of sound and style only.

quiz.q: The stressed pronoun matching indefinite on is…
quiz.why: Chacun pour soi; on est bien chez soi.
Nous autres is the Quebec stressed 'we'.

quiz.q: 'On a retrouvé la voiture volée.' What's the best translation?
quiz.why: On can mean we or an unknown agent; context decides.
